events.limitations: The total penalty was not allocated solely to Epstein. Regulatory compliance findings differ from criminal convictions.

events.title: DOJ criticizes handling of the non-prosecution deal
events.summary: OPR found Acosta exercised poor judgment and victims were not treated with expected candor and sensitivity; it did not find professional misconduct by DOJ attorneys.
events.limitations: This was an internal professional-responsibility review, with a specific remit and legal standard.

events.title: Jury convicts Maxwell
events.summary: A federal jury found Maxwell guilty on five counts concerning the recruitment, transportation and trafficking of minors with Epstein.
events.limitations: She was acquitted on one tried count; the court later treated three conspiracy counts as multiplicitous for judgment.

events.title: Maxwell receives a 20-year prison sentence
events.summary: The court sentenced Maxwell to 240 months for her role in the abuse scheme.
events.limitations: United States v. Maxwell, 20 Cr. 330. Conviction and sentence are adjudicated facts.

events.title: Inspector General documents detention failures
events.summary: DOJ OIG reported serious failures in supervision, records and recording systems during Epstein's detention.
events.limitations: The report did not establish homicide; it found no evidence contradicting the FBI's conclusion about the death.

events.title: JPMorgan settles USVI civil case
events.summary: JPMorgan agreed to pay $75 million to resolve the Virgin Islands' Epstein-related civil lawsuit.
events.limitations: Case 1:22-cv-10904 (SDNY). Settlement resolved allegations without a trial; it is not a criminal conviction.

events.title: JPMorgan survivor settlement receives final approval
events.summary: JPMorgan's issuer disclosure records final approval of a $290 million settlement paid to a survivor fund.
events.limitations: Doe 1 v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, 1:22-cv-10019 (JSR). A civil settlement, not a criminal conviction.

events.title: DOJ releases first-phase records
events.summary: DOJ announced publication of records including flight logs and a redacted contact book.
events.limitations: A flight-log entry, contact-book listing or document mention does not establish participation in a crime.

events.title: DOJ and FBI publish review conclusions
events.summary: The agencies said their review found no incriminating client list or credible evidence of blackmail of prominent people.
events.limitations: Agency conclusions quoted in the court's August 11 order, p. 7. This is a dated statement about that review, not a claim that every historical allegation has been adjudicated.

events.title: DOJ announces a much larger files release
events.summary: DOJ reported nearly 3.5 million released pages in total, together with more than 2,000 videos and 180,000 images.
events.limitations: Counts are DOJ's stated production totals. DOJ warned the corpus includes potentially false public submissions. This dataset does not claim to have reviewed the whole release.

events.title: Court denies Maxwell's post-conviction petition
events.summary: Judge Paul Engelmayer denied Maxwell's section 2255 challenge, including arguments based on newly released Epstein materials.
events.limitations: Maxwell v. United States, 25 Civ. 10468 (PAE), Dkt. 10. This identifies the specific ruling, without predicting future proceedings.

events.title: East India Company receives a royal charter
events.summary: Elizabeth I granted London merchants exclusive English trading rights east of the Cape of Good Hope.
events.limitations: Historical context does not establish institutional continuity with modern companies.

events.title: Bank of England founded
events.summary: Private subscribers financed a £1.2 million government loan, establishing the Bank of England.

events.title: Parliament regulates East India Company governance
events.summary: Parliamentary inquiries and financial difficulties produced legislation supervising the Company’s Indian administration.

events.title: Government of India Act transfers rule to the Crown
events.summary: The Act transferred governance of Company-held Indian territories to the Crown.
events.limitations: This dates a statutory transfer; it is not the Company’s dissolution date.

events.title: Federal Reserve Act signed
events.summary: President Woodrow Wilson signed the legislation establishing the Federal Reserve System.

events.title: Bretton Woods delegates design monetary institutions
events.summary: Delegates from 44 countries agreed to establish the IMF and the institution that became the World Bank.
events.limitations: Conference agreements and later legal commencement are different milestones.

events.title: Bank of England enters public ownership
events.summary: The Bank was nationalized and became wholly owned by the UK government.
events.limitations: Founding private stockholders are not evidence of present private ownership.

events.title: CIA formally established
events.summary: The National Security Act created an independent civilian foreign intelligence agency.

events.title: UN recommends partition of Mandatory Palestine
events.summary: General Assembly Resolution 181 recommended Arab and Jewish states with a special international regime for Jerusalem.
events.limitations: A recommendation is not proof of implementation or a complete account of the ensuing conflict.

events.title: U.S. leadership approves Iran covert-operation plan
events.summary: A declassified record identifies approval by the president, Secretary of State and CIA director for the campaign against Mosaddeq’s government.
events.limitations: Approval date; not the later coup date. Surviving released records are incomplete.

events.title: CIA assists overthrow of Árbenz government
events.summary: The State Department’s historical account acknowledges CIA assistance in removing Guatemala’s elected president.
events.limitations: Documents one operation, not a theory about all later Guatemalan events.

events.title: Dartmouth AI summer project proposed
events.summary: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon proposed a 1956 research project on machine intelligence.
events.limitations: The proposal’s appended mailing list is explicitly not a complete attendance list.

events.title: Church Committee investigates intelligence abuses
events.summary: The Senate investigated intelligence-agency misconduct and held public hearings in September and October.
events.limitations: Individual programs and agency conduct require their own records; this is not a generic “black ops” label.

events.title: Senate holds MKULTRA hearing
events.summary: CIA Director Stansfield Turner testified after additional records of the agency’s behavioral-research program were recovered.
events.limitations: Records were incomplete; the hearing does not prove claims about contemporary individuals.

events.title: BlackRock founded
events.summary: Eight founders, including Larry Fink, established the New York asset manager.
events.limitations: BlackRock and Blackwater are unrelated entities in this dataset; similar names do not establish a relationship.

events.title: NVIDIA founded
events.summary: Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem founded NVIDIA.

events.title: CIA establishes In-Q-Tel
events.summary: CIA established IQT as an independent nonprofit investor to connect private-sector technology with government needs.
events.limitations: IQT explicitly says it is not a government entity or a division of CIA.

events.title: Palantir incorporated
events.summary: Palantir’s SEC filing records incorporation in Delaware on this date.
events.limitations: Incorporation, operational launch and individual employment start dates need not coincide.

events.title: NVIDIA introduces CUDA
events.summary: CUDA expanded access to GPU parallel processing for research and general computation.

events.title: Nisur Square shooting
events.summary: DOJ’s case account records Blackwater guards killing 14 unarmed civilians and wounding others in Baghdad.
events.limitations: This is the charged incident described by DOJ; later sentences and pardons are separate events.

events.title: DeepMind launched
events.summary: DeepMind’s account dates the launch of its AI research organization to 2010.

events.title: USTC acquires Xe training and support businesses
events.summary: The acquisition covered selected operations, excluding Blackwater intellectual property and other businesses.

events.title: Acquired operations adopt Academi name
events.summary: The purchased training and security operations were renamed Academi.

events.title: Turning Point USA founded
events.summary: TPUSA’s handbook dates Charlie Kirk’s founding of the organization to 5 June 2012.

events.title: Constellis Holdings formed
events.summary: A consolidation brought Academi, Triple Canopy and other businesses into the Constellis platform.

events.title: Senate releases CIA detention study summary
events.summary: The Senate Intelligence Committee published its executive summary, findings, additional views and related materials on CIA detention and interrogation.
events.limitations: Findings, minority views and the CIA response must be attributed separately.

events.title: OpenAI launches
events.summary: The launch announcement identified Sam Altman and Elon Musk as co-chairs and named Peter Thiel and AWS among funding supporters.
events.limitations: Funding commitments at launch are not a current ownership, board or payment ledger.

events.title: Congressional record identifies Candace Owens’s TPUSA role
events.summary: The House Judiciary Committee’s witness list identifies Owens as Turning Point USA director of communications.
events.limitations: This establishes the role on the hearing date, not her complete employment history.

events.title: U.S. indicts twelve Russian military-intelligence officers
events.summary: DOJ announced charges alleging hacking and staged releases intended to interfere with the 2016 U.S. election.
events.limitations: Charges are allegations. This indictment did not allege a knowing American participant.

events.title: Charlie Kirk establishes Turning Point Action
events.summary: TPUSA’s biography identifies Turning Point Action as a separate 501(c)(4) founded by Kirk in 2019.

events.title: Three former Blackwater guards resentenced
events.summary: Paul Slough, Evan Liberty and Dustin Heard received new prison terms for their roles in the Nisur Square shooting.
events.limitations: All three subsequently received presidential pardons in December 2020.

events.title: Candace Owens appears as congressional witness
events.summary: The House hearing record identifies Owens as BLEXIT founder and a show host.
events.limitations: Witness status does not imply endorsement of testimony by Congress.

events.title: Palantir filing discloses founder voting structure
events.summary: The S-1 described a proposed founder voting arrangement for Alex Karp, Stephen Cohen and Peter Thiel.
events.limitations: This is a dated disclosure, not a claim that current ownership is unchanged.

events.title: Trump pardons four former Blackwater contractors
events.summary: The White House announced full pardons for Nicholas Slatten, Paul Slough, Evan Liberty and Dustin Heard.
events.limitations: Clemency is distinct from an acquittal or an independent finding that the shooting was lawful.

events.title: Google announces Nimbus cloud selection
events.summary: Google announced selection to provide cloud services under the Israeli government’s Nimbus procurement.
events.limitations: Cloud procurement alone does not identify individual operational uses.

events.title: UN General Assembly demands Russian withdrawal
events.summary: A resolution affirming Ukrainian sovereignty and demanding an end to the offensive passed with 141 votes in favor.
events.limitations: A General Assembly resolution is distinct from a criminal judgment against individuals.

events.title: Zelenskyy and Fink discuss reconstruction advice
events.summary: The Ukrainian presidency described discussions about BlackRock providing pro bono advice on structuring a reconstruction fund.
events.limitations: Advisory discussions do not establish ownership of Ukraine, its land or its government.

events.title: Israeli Finance Ministry announces local Google cloud zone
events.summary: The ministry said Google’s local cloud zone was operating and identified AWS as another Nimbus tender winner.
events.limitations: The release includes government and security-sector coverage, but not a list of specific missions.

events.title: Microsoft expands OpenAI partnership
events.summary: Microsoft announced a multiyear, multibillion-dollar investment following earlier investments in 2019 and 2021.
events.limitations: Historical announcement; the amount and later terms should not be inferred from this record.

events.title: U.S. Treasury designates Wagner a transnational criminal organization
events.summary: Treasury announced sanctions against Wagner and parts of its support network.
events.limitations: A U.S. sanctions finding is not a criminal conviction; attribution is to Treasury.

events.title: TPUSA announces BLEXIT partnership
events.summary: TPUSA said its resources, leadership and board would support BLEXIT; co-founders Owens and Tatum would remain involved.
events.limitations: The announcement establishes an organizational partnership, not agreement on every later statement.

events.title: ICC issues warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova
events.summary: The Court issued arrest warrants alleging unlawful deportation and transfer of children from occupied Ukrainian areas.
events.limitations: Warrants are allegations of individual responsibility, not convictions or collective guilt.

events.title: Google DeepMind announced
events.summary: Google combined DeepMind and the Google Brain team in a new Google DeepMind unit.

events.title: Ukraine ministry and Palantir sign memorandum
events.summary: The agreement covered defense and reconstruction cooperation, including damage assessment and reconstruction software.
events.limitations: The memorandum does not identify every later deployment or military decision.

events.title: Amazon and Anthropic announce investment partnership
events.summary: Amazon committed to invest up to $4 billion; the companies announced cloud and chip collaboration.
events.limitations: The announced ceiling is not an assertion that the full amount was paid on this date.

events.title: BlackRock, GIP, Microsoft and MGX launch AI infrastructure partnership
events.summary: The partners proposed data-center and power investment, seeking $30 billion in equity and up to $100 billion including debt; NVIDIA would supply expertise.
events.limitations: Fundraising objectives are not completed investment totals.

events.title: Anthropic, Palantir and AWS announce government AI partnership
events.summary: The companies announced access to Claude through Palantir on AWS for U.S. defense and intelligence work.
events.limitations: Does not establish specific agency use, targeting decisions or involvement in particular incidents.

events.title: Amazon expands Anthropic investment
events.summary: Anthropic announced another $4 billion from Amazon, bringing the announced total to $8 billion, and named AWS its primary training partner.
events.limitations: Amazon was described as a minority investor; commercial partnership is not sole ownership.

events.title: Erika Kirk selected to lead TPUSA
events.summary: AP reported the board unanimously elected Erika Kirk CEO and board chair; TPUSA’s biography confirms those roles.
events.limitations: Professional succession and marriage do not establish unrelated intelligence or criminal affiliations.

events.title: BIBLEin365 publishes a live Q&A with Erika Kirk and James Kaddis
events.summary: The publisher’s episode description identifies Kirk as ministry leader and Kaddis as pastoral advisor.
events.limitations: A documented media/ministry collaboration; no broader affiliation inferred.

events.title: BlackRock Advisors settles SEC conflict-disclosure action
events.summary: The adviser accepted a $12 million penalty and compliance review over undisclosed portfolio-manager conflicts.
events.limitations: Settled administrative findings; neither admission nor criminal conviction.

events.title: BlackRock settles whistleblower-award waiver action
events.summary: SEC ordered a $340,000 penalty over separation agreements waiving whistleblower awards.
events.limitations: No identified instance of a prevented SEC communication or enforcement of the clause.

events.title: BlackRock Advisors settles fund-disclosure case
events.summary: SEC imposed a $2.5 million penalty for inaccurate Aviron investment descriptions and interest-rate reporting.
events.limitations: The adviser corrected disclosures in 2019; no admission or denial.

events.title: NVIDIA settles SEC cryptomining-disclosure action
events.summary: NVIDIA accepted a $5.5 million penalty concerning two fiscal-2018 quarterly reports.
events.limitations: Concerns securities disclosure, not AI model safety.

events.title: FTC files Ring privacy and security allegations
events.summary: FTC alleged excessive internal video access, algorithm training without consent and inadequate account security.
events.limitations: Complaint allegations resolved by consent order, not tried findings.

events.title: Court enters Ring privacy consent order
events.summary: The order requires $5.8 million, security safeguards and deletion of defined recordings and derived work products.
events.limitations: Specific deletion categories and exceptions are defined in the order.

events.title: Alexa privacy settlement announced
events.summary: DOJ and FTC alleged excessive retention and ineffective deletion of children’s voice and other user data.
events.limitations: Use of retained data in algorithm improvement was an agency allegation.

events.title: Court enters Alexa privacy consent order
events.summary: FTC’s docket records entry of the settlement governing deletion, data uses and a $25 million penalty.
events.limitations: Amazon disputed the alleged violations.

events.title: Facebook agrees to $5 billion privacy settlement
events.summary: The agreement resolved FTC allegations that Facebook violated its 2012 privacy order.
events.limitations: Cambridge Analytica enforcement was related but separate.

events.title: FTC finalizes Facebook privacy-order modification
events.summary: FTC approved the revised administrative privacy order incorporating the 2019 settlement.
events.limitations: Later proposed modifications are separate proceedings.

events.title: Microsoft announces Xbox privacy settlement
events.summary: The $20 million agreement addressed FTC allegations about children’s account data, consent and retention.
events.limitations: FTC’s 2024 update confirms court entry and payment; this date is the announcement.

events.title: Court finds Google unlawfully maintained search monopolies
events.summary: The court found Sherman Act liability in general search services and general search text advertising.
events.limitations: Civil trial finding; subsequent appeals are included below.

events.title: Google search remedies enter final district-court judgment
events.summary: The judgment imposes distribution restrictions, qualified data access and syndication duties.
events.limitations: Final district-court judgment does not mean appeals are exhausted.

events.title: Court denies Google’s partial stay request without prejudice
events.summary: The court declined to pause data-sharing and syndication provisions at that stage, permitting a renewed request after advance notice.
events.limitations: A stay ruling is not an appellate decision on liability.

events.title: United States files Google search cross-appeal brief
events.summary: The government filed a response and opening cross-appeal brief in D.C. Circuit cases 26-5023, 26-5047 and 26-5049.
events.limitations: Party arguments are not appellate findings.

events.title: Amazon Prime settlement enters court order
events.summary: Amazon’s consent settlement provides a $1 billion penalty, $1.5 billion redress fund and enrollment/cancellation changes.
events.limitations: Neither admission nor denial; separate from Amazon’s antitrust case.

events.title: Amazon Prime refund procedure is revised
events.summary: The revised order expands automatic payments and conditionally permits supplemental distributions capped at $200 total per eligible consumer.
events.limitations: The cap is not a guarantee that every consumer receives $200; conditions and phases apply.

events.title: Palantir hiring-discrimination settlement announced
events.summary: DOL announced a consent decree providing $1,659,434 in relief and eight job offers.
events.limitations: Palantir denied the allegations; this was a settlement, not a contested merits judgment.

events.title: CIA approves MKULTRA
events.summary: The Senate hearing's documentary appendix records approval of the research program.
events.limitations: Approval of research does not establish that its experimental objectives were achieved.

events.title: MKULTRA records destroyed
events.summary: Turner's later testimony described destruction authorized by the then CIA director; financial records survived separately.
events.limitations: The surviving archive cannot reconstruct every subject or operation.

events.title: FBI terminates COINTELPRO
events.summary: The FBI's historical account dates termination of the programs to April 1971.
events.limitations: Ending a named program does not resolve every underlying civil-rights claim.

events.title: Church Committee issues final report
events.summary: The Senate inquiry found intelligence agencies had undermined constitutional rights and recommended stronger oversight.
events.limitations: Legislative findings; individual criminal liability requires separate evidence.

events.title: FBI begins Iran-Contra investigation
events.summary: The attorney general ordered an investigation after disclosure that Iran arms-sale proceeds had been diverted to the Contras.
events.limitations: Opening an investigation was not a finding against every official involved.

events.title: Iran-Contra defendants indicted
events.summary: A grand jury indicted North, Poindexter, Albert Hakim and Richard Secord. Their cases had different outcomes.
events.limitations: North and Poindexter's later convictions were vacated; Hakim and Secord pleaded guilty.

events.title: Bush grants six Iran-Contra pardons
events.summary: Pardons covered Weinberger, Elliott Abrams, Duane Clarridge, Alan Fiers, Clair George and Robert McFarlane.
events.limitations: Weinberger and Clarridge were pardoned before trial.

events.title: Walsh submits Iran-Contra final report
events.summary: The independent counsel submitted his report after prosecutions, reversals and pardons.
events.limitations: The inquiry did not yield a uniform outcome for all defendants.

events.title: FBI issues detainee-interrogation policy
events.summary: OIG later found this guidance late and insufficiently clear about reporting other agencies' mistreatment.
events.limitations: The review generally credited FBI agents for avoiding abuse.

events.title: OIG reports on FBI detainee interrogations
events.summary: The inspector general identified shortcomings in guidance and escalation of concerns about other agencies.
events.limitations: The OIG did not substantiate allegations of FBI participation in detainee abuse.

events.title: DOJ closes investigations into two detainee deaths
events.summary: DOJ declined prosecution, stating that admissible evidence could not sustain convictions beyond reasonable doubt.
events.limitations: A charging decision is distinct from the Senate's later findings and from an acquittal after trial.

events.title: CIA responds to draft Senate detention findings
events.summary: The agency acknowledged management failures but disputed central conclusions about effectiveness and deliberate misrepresentation.
events.limitations: The memorandum was approved for public release in December 2014; it is the agency's response.

events.title: Xe agrees to export-control civil settlement
events.summary: The later filed DPA records a $42 million State Department consent agreement.
events.limitations: Civil administrative settlement; this entry is not a criminal conviction.

events.title: Academi enters deferred prosecution agreement
events.summary: The agreement acknowledged corporate conduct and specified a $7.5 million penalty with compliance-cost credits.
events.limitations: DPA, not conviction; later dismissal is separately reported.

events.title: Academi deferred charges reportedly dismissed
events.summary: The Intercept reported that charges were dismissed after the government certified compliance.
events.limitations: Secondary report reproduced by Reader Supported News; final dismissal order not retrieved.

events.title: Appeals court reverses Slatten conviction and orders resentencing
events.summary: The court ordered a separate retrial for Slatten and new sentences for Slough, Liberty and Heard.
events.limitations: Slatten was later reconvicted; all four were pardoned in 2020.

events.title: Slatten sentenced to life after retrial
events.summary: Following a 2018 mistrial and subsequent guilty verdict, Slatten received a life sentence for first-degree murder.
events.limitations: President Trump granted a full pardon in December 2020.

events.title: U.S. announces destructive-malware indictment
events.summary: Six officers of GRU Unit 74455 were charged in an indictment returned October 15.
events.limitations: The alleged conduct remains an accusation in this record, not a trial finding.

events.title: Federal officers charged over falsified prison-monitoring records
events.summary: DOJ announced an indictment alleging that two MCC employees falsified records of required inmate checks on the night of Epstein's death. The case concerned monitoring records and conspiracy to falsify them.
events.limitations: An indictment is an accusation. These charges were later dismissed after deferred-prosecution agreements; this record does not imply a conviction or a homicide charge.

events.title: Monitoring-record case enters deferred-prosecution agreements
events.summary: The later dismissal filing records agreements on or about May 20 requiring a six-month period of compliance. OIG reports that the employees admitted falsely certifying checks and agreed to cooperate and complete community service.
events.limitations: A deferred-prosecution agreement is not a trial conviction. May 20 is the approximate agreement date recited in docket 65; the OIG report describes the agreements under May 25. The later dismissal is separately dated.

events.title: Dismissal filed after prison employees complete agreements
events.summary: Docket 65 in 19 Cr. 830 records the nolle-prosequi disposition after prosecutors reported that the employees completed the deferred-prosecution terms. The criminal case ended without convictions.
events.limitations: January 3 is the court filing date. The prosecutor's recommendation was dated December 13, 2021, the date used in OIG's later narrative. Dismissal does not erase the agreements' admissions or the OIG's administrative findings.

events.title: Court approves Deutsche Bank's $75 million survivor settlement
events.summary: Judge Jed Rakoff approved the class settlement in 22-cv-10018 and dismissed the released claims with prejudice. The judgment specifies a $75 million obligation to the qualified settlement fund.
events.limitations: Paragraph 11 explicitly prevents treating the settlement as an admission or evidence of liability or wrongdoing. Paragraph 12 specifies the payment obligation, not proof of completed distributions to claimants.

events.title: Second Circuit affirms Maxwell's criminal judgment
events.summary: The court affirmed the June 29, 2022 judgment, rejecting the appellate challenges it considered, including Maxwell's claim that Epstein's Florida non-prosecution agreement barred her New York prosecution.
events.limitations: The opinion resolves Maxwell's appeal and the issues presented. It does not adjudicate allegations about every person named in Epstein-related documents.

events.title: Supreme Court declines Maxwell's petition
events.summary: Supreme Court docket 24-1073 records denial of Maxwell's petition for certiorari following the Second Circuit decision.
events.limitations: Denial of certiorari does not supply a new Supreme Court merits ruling. This event describes that petition only, not the availability or outcome of every later collateral challenge.

events.title: MIT reports progress on donor and reporting reforms
events.summary: President Reif described work on controversial-donor policies, whistleblower and retaliation protections, campus visitors and Media Lab governance following the Epstein review.
events.limitations: This is MIT's account of its response. Some measures remained under development; the letter does not independently establish their effectiveness.

events.title: Harvard announces policy findings and sanctions concerning Nowak
events.summary: According to the dean's letter reported by Harvard Magazine, an FAS review found policy violations involving professional conduct, campus access and endorsements. Harvard closed the Program for Evolutionary Dynamics and restricted Nowak's research and advising for two years.
events.limitations: University disciplinary findings are not criminal convictions. The corrected report says Nowak retained both departmental appointments. Later restoration of privileges and a separately reported 2026 review must be read as distinct developments.

events.title: Nowak's research and advising privileges restored
events.summary: The Harvard Crimson reported in May that a department chair confirmed restoration of Nowak's privileges in March after the two-year restrictions.
events.limitations: The exact March date was not supplied. Restoration is not reported as a reversal of the original policy findings; it should not be described as exoneration.

events.title: Harvard Magazine reports renewed leave pending review
events.summary: A Harvard spokesperson confirmed Nowak was on paid administrative leave while the university reviewed newly released Epstein-related documents. The dean said arrangements were being made for teaching and advising responsibilities.
events.limitations: Date is publication, not a verified effective date. The institution had not disclosed specific grounds, and the report said Nowak was not accused of a crime. No outcome of this new review was verified.

relationships.label: FAS imposed two-year research and advising restrictions
relationships.context: Reported sanctions followed an internal policy review. A department chair later confirmed restoration of privileges in March 2023.
relationships.limitations: The edge records a university action, not criminal complicity. It does not mean the 2021 restrictions remain in force.

cases.title: BlackRock Advisors: undisclosed outside-business conflict
cases.summary: SEC settlement concerning a portfolio manager’s outside energy business.
cases.statusDetail: Settled SEC administrative order, April 2015.
cases.findings: SEC found undisclosed conflicts and deficient controls involving the manager’s Rice Energy interest and a fund investment.
cases.response: The adviser neither admitted nor denied the findings.
cases.outcome: $12 million penalty, censure, cease-and-desist relief and independent compliance review.
cases.limitations: The respondent was BlackRock Advisors, LLC. The order does not establish criminal guilt or misconduct by unrelated group companies.

cases.title: BlackRock: separation agreements and whistleblower incentives
cases.summary: SEC action over award-waiver language used from 2011 to 2016.
cases.statusDetail: Settled administrative order under Rule 21F-17.
cases.findings: SEC found that award waivers undermined incentives for reporting potential securities violations.
cases.response: BlackRock neither admitted nor denied findings; it had revised the agreement before SEC staff contacted it.
cases.outcome: $340,000 civil penalty and remedial measures, including annual training.
cases.limitations: SEC identified no instance in which the clause stopped a communication or BlackRock enforced it. No criminal finding.

cases.title: BlackRock Advisors: Aviron investment disclosures
cases.summary: SEC order addresses publicly filed fund reports from 2015–2019.
cases.statusDetail: Settled SEC administrative findings.
cases.findings: SEC found that reports misclassified film-finance business Aviron and overstated its interest rate.
cases.response: BlackRock neither admitted nor denied findings. It identified and corrected the inaccuracies in 2019.
cases.outcome: $2.5 million penalty, censure and cease-and-desist order.
cases.limitations: This disclosure action is distinct from the separate case against Aviron’s founder. It does not attribute his misconduct to the adviser.

cases.title: NVIDIA: cryptomining’s effect on gaming revenue
cases.summary: SEC found omissions about a material driver of GPU revenue growth.
cases.statusDetail: Settled SEC order, release 33-11060.
cases.findings: The order found inadequate disclosure and controls concerning cryptomining demand in two fiscal-2018 quarters.
cases.response: NVIDIA consented without admitting or denying the findings.
cases.outcome: $5.5 million civil penalty and cease-and-desist order.
cases.limitations: The cited Securities Act provisions can rest on negligence; this is not a criminal conviction or resolution of separate investor litigation.

cases.title: Ring: private videos, algorithm training and account security
cases.summary: Court-approved settlement of FTC privacy and security allegations.
cases.statusDetail: Entered stipulated order, docket 12.
cases.findings: FTC alleged unauthorized video access and training uses, alongside security failures; these allegations were resolved without trial.
cases.response: Ring neither admitted nor denied the allegations and waived appeal of the consent order.
cases.outcome: $5.8 million judgment; privacy/security program and deletion of defined pre-March-2018 recordings and affected models or algorithms.
cases.limitations: The decree establishes obligations, not criminal guilt. It does not implicate every employee or all later Ring products.

cases.title: Amazon Alexa: children’s recordings and deletion requests
cases.summary: Entered settlement addressing retention and deletion of Alexa data.
cases.statusDetail: Court entry verified in FTC docket, July 19, 2023.
cases.findings: The complaint alleged COPPA and deception violations, including retention after deletion requests and use to improve algorithms.
cases.response: Amazon denied violating the law and described parental controls and planned deletion changes.
cases.outcome: $25 million penalty, deletion requirements, a ban on using information covered by deletion requests to develop or improve data products, and privacy-program obligations.
cases.limitations: Settlement of disputed allegations, not a trial finding. The case does not adjudicate Amazon’s unrelated services.

cases.title: Facebook: privacy controls and the 2019 FTC settlement
cases.summary: $5 billion agreement addressing alleged violations of an earlier privacy order.
cases.statusDetail: Settlement announced in 2019; FTC order modification finalized April 28, 2020.
cases.findings: FTC alleged deceptive privacy settings, third-party app access and misrepresentations concerning facial recognition and advertising uses.
cases.response: Facebook neither admitted nor denied allegations; its statement acknowledged a breach of trust and promised stronger privacy controls.
cases.outcome: $5 billion civil penalty and strengthened privacy governance, independent oversight and certifications.
cases.limitations: Cambridge Analytica was separately prosecuted administratively. This case does not establish every Cambridge Analytica allegation or decide later Meta disputes.

cases.title: Microsoft Xbox: children’s account data
cases.summary: COPPA settlement covering notice, parental consent and retention.
cases.statusDetail: Announced June 2023; FTC’s 2024 update confirms an entered federal order and payment.
cases.findings: FTC alleged premature collection, incomplete notices and excessive retention of children’s personal data.
cases.response: No-admission terms appear in the stipulation. Microsoft said it fixed a retention glitch, deleted data and strengthened controls.
cases.outcome: $20 million penalty and changes to consent, deletion and disclosures to game publishers.
cases.limitations: Microsoft’s glitch explanation is its response, not the entirety of FTC’s allegations. No criminal finding or ruling on unrelated Microsoft products.

cases.title: Google: search-distribution monopolization
cases.summary: Civil trial findings followed by remedies and appellate proceedings.
cases.statusDetail: District-court liability and December 2025 judgment; 2026 appeal and cross-appeals documented. No appellate disposition verified here.
cases.findings: The court found unlawful monopoly maintenance in general search services and general search text advertising.
cases.response: Google disputes the decision, emphasizing product quality, user choice and competition, and appealed in January 2026.
cases.outcome: Distribution restrictions and data-sharing/syndication remedies; May 2026 partial-stay request denied without prejudice.
cases.limitations: Do not call this an unappealable final outcome. The government’s July 2026 brief is advocacy. The separate ad-tech case is outside this record.

cases.title: Amazon Prime: enrollment and cancellation
cases.summary: Consent settlement over allegedly deceptive subscription flows.
cases.statusDetail: Entered September 2025 order; redress procedure revised September 2026.
cases.findings: FTC alleged enrollment without informed consent and deliberately difficult cancellation processes.
cases.response: The order states defendants neither admit nor deny the complaint allegations.
cases.outcome: $1 billion civil penalty, $1.5 billion consumer-redress fund and interface changes; later order expands automatic refunds.
cases.limitations: Consumer eligibility and supplemental payments are conditional. This settlement does not decide the separate Amazon antitrust action or imply all subscriptions were unauthorized.

cases.title: Palantir: engineering-applicant hiring practices
cases.summary: Consent decree resolving OFCCP’s historical hiring-discrimination allegations.
cases.statusDetail: DOL announced the consent decree April 25, 2017.
cases.findings: OFCCP alleged race-based adverse impact against Asian applicants for three engineering job categories at Palo Alto.
cases.response: Palantir denied the allegations and offered alternative statistical analyses disputing adverse impact.
cases.outcome: $1,659,434 in back wages and other relief, including stock-option value, plus eight offers of employment.
cases.limitations: Resolved by consent, not a litigated discrimination finding. Historical executive-order duties must not be presented as a statement of current policy.

cases.title: CIA detention and coercive interrogation: Senate findings
cases.summary: The Senate examined CIA detention and interrogation after September 11.

entityRoles.role: Program operator and subject of inquiry

cases.statusDetail: Dated to public release of the Senate study; legislative findings, not criminal convictions.
cases.findings: The committee found brutality, misleading descriptions and ineffective coercive interrogation. It identified at least 119 detainees, including at least 26 held outside the program's detention standard.
cases.response: CIA acknowledged management, accountability and contractor-conflict failures, but disputed conclusions about unique intelligence and deliberate deception. Separate Senate minority views are linked from the release.
cases.outcome: CIA's response said the program ended in 2009 and described reforms. DOJ's separate 2012 investigation into two deaths ended without charges for insufficient admissible evidence.
cases.limitations: The full study remained classified in the cited release; findings and rebuttals must be attributed separately. DOJ closure does not reverse the legislative findings.

cases.title: FBI detainee-interrogation oversight: failures and limits
cases.summary: DOJ's inspector general reviewed FBI conduct in Guantanamo, Afghanistan and Iraq.

entityRoles.role: Agency reviewed; agents also reported concerns

cases.statusDetail: May 2008 OIG review, not an adjudication of every reported incident.
cases.findings: OIG found inadequate and delayed guidance and failures to resolve agents' concerns about other agencies' harsh techniques.
cases.response: Mueller directed in 2002 that FBI agents avoid joint interrogations using prohibited FBI techniques.
cases.outcome: OIG found no support for allegations of FBI detainee abuse and said the vast majority of agents adhered to FBI policy.
cases.limitations: OIG noted infrequent departures from normal domestic techniques, while finding no support for abuse allegations. Observing another agency's conduct does not establish participation or supply individual criminal judgments.

cases.title: MKULTRA: nonconsensual drug experiments and destroyed records
cases.summary: A Senate hearing examined recovered CIA behavioral-research records.
cases.statusDetail: 1977 sworn testimony and documentary record; not a current-operations finding.
cases.findings: The record describes covert drug testing on unwitting people and funding through research institutions.
cases.response: Turner disclosed recovered financial records and agreed to notify identifiable subjects and institutions.
cases.outcome: The hearing exposed additional activity despite destruction of operational records in 1973.
cases.limitations: Some researchers and institutions were unaware of CIA sponsorship. Experiments do not establish successful mind control; incomplete records prevent a complete victim or operation list.

cases.title: COINTELPRO: political disruption and civil-rights abuses
cases.summary: The Church Committee documented FBI efforts to disrupt political and civil-rights activity.
cases.statusDetail: 1976 legislative findings, with later FBI acknowledgment.
cases.findings: The inquiry described efforts to discredit civil-rights and antiwar organizations and individuals, including Martin Luther King Jr.
cases.response: The FBI's retrospective acknowledges infringement of First Amendment rights. Senator Tower accepted that excesses occurred while cautioning against excessive restraints on national-security discretion.
cases.outcome: COINTELPRO ended in April 1971; the later inquiry contributed to permanent congressional intelligence oversight and other reforms.
cases.limitations: This case concerns specific historical programs, not every FBI employee or contemporary investigation.

cases.title: Iran-Contra prosecutions, vacated convictions and pardons
cases.summary: An independent counsel investigated arms transactions and diversion of proceeds to the Contras.
cases.statusDetail: Dated to Walsh's final report; individual cases had distinct dispositions.
cases.findings: NARA records guilty pleas and convictions arising from the investigation, as well as cases ending without sustained convictions.
cases.response: North and Poindexter's convictions were vacated because of taint from immunized congressional testimony. Bush defended his pardons as a response to politicized prosecutions.
cases.outcome: Bush pardoned six men in December 1992, including Weinberger and Clarridge before trial; Walsh submitted his report in August 1993.
cases.limitations: Vacated convictions cannot be presented as standing convictions. A pardon before trial does not establish the charged allegations.

cases.title: Nisur Square: convictions, appeal, retrial and pardons
cases.summary: Four former Blackwater guards faced U.S. prosecutions over the 2007 Baghdad shootings.
cases.statusDetail: Historical convictions and 2019 sentences; all four defendants received full presidential pardons on December 22, 2020.
cases.findings: Slatten was convicted of first-degree murder after retrial. Slough, Liberty and Heard were convicted of manslaughter, attempted manslaughter and firearms offenses.
cases.response: The 2017 appeal found Slatten should have received a separate trial and required resentencing of the others; the court included separate opinions.
cases.outcome: Slatten received life in August 2019; the others received 180, 168 and 151 months in September. Trump subsequently pardoned all four.
cases.limitations: The record does not establish criminal liability of every employee or company owner. The pardons are executive acts, distinct from the jury verdicts.

cases.title: Blackwater/Xe export-control settlement and Academi DPA
cases.summary: Corporate export and firearms enforcement produced a civil settlement and a later deferred prosecution agreement.
cases.statusDetail: 2010 State Department settlement; a separate 2012 DPA resolved criminal charges conditionally, without a conviction.
cases.findings: The corporate agreement accepted responsibility for its statement of facts involving unauthorized exports, defense services and firearms conduct.
cases.response: DOJ acknowledged cooperation, replacement of leadership and improved compliance controls.
cases.outcome: The civil penalty was $42 million. The DPA specified $7.5 million with up to $2.5 million in compliance credits. A 2016 Intercept report says deferred charges were dismissed in September 2015 after compliance.
cases.limitations: The dismissal is reported through a reproduction; its court order was not retrieved. Corporate admissions do not establish personal guilt of shareholders. No active prosecution or corporate conviction is claimed.

cases.title: Wagner: U.S. sanctions findings concerning serious abuses
cases.summary: Treasury designated Wagner a significant transnational criminal organization.
cases.statusDetail: January 2023 administrative sanctions determination, not a criminal conviction.
cases.findings: Treasury attributed mass executions, rape, child abductions and physical abuse in Mali and the Central African Republic to Wagner personnel.
cases.response: The cited Treasury announcement contains no substantive response from Wagner.
cases.outcome: Treasury redesignated Wagner under transnational-crime and Central African Republic sanctions authorities.
cases.limitations: This entry records the 2023 decision, not a complete or current sanctions register. It does not assign responsibility to every Russian person or every contractor.

cases.title: Twelve GRU officers: 2016 election-hacking allegations
cases.summary: A U.S. indictment alleged hacking and release of stolen political documents.
cases.statusDetail: July 2018 indictment; this case card does not represent a conviction or a current docket certification.
cases.findings: Prosecutors alleged spearphishing, theft, staged releases and attempts to obtain election-administration data.
cases.response: The cited announcement contains no defense pleading and expressly states the presumption of innocence.
cases.outcome: Twelve named officers were charged; the verified source records the indictment rather than a trial outcome.
cases.limitations: DOJ said this indictment did not allege knowing American participation or changes to vote counts or the election outcome. Institutional affiliation does not make every member a defendant.

cases.title: GRU Unit 74455: destructive-malware allegations
cases.summary: U.S. prosecutors charged six officers over alleged cyberattacks affecting civilian infrastructure and public events.
cases.statusDetail: October 2020 indictment and announcement; no trial verdict is represented.
cases.findings: The indictment alleged Ukrainian power-grid attacks, NotPetya damage, election-related hacking and disruption of the 2018 Winter Olympics.
cases.response: The charging release contains no defense response and states that the defendants are presumed innocent.
cases.outcome: Six officers were charged. Anatoliy Kovalev was also a defendant in the separate 2018 election case.
cases.limitations: Charges are allegations, and affiliation is not collective guilt. This research does not certify the current docket or custody status.

cases.title: Ghislaine Maxwell: conviction, sentence and reviewed appeals
cases.summary: Maxwell received a 20-year sentence following the jury verdict in the federal prosecution concerning her participation in Epstein's abuse of minors.
cases.statusDetail: June 28, 2022 sentencing hearing; judgment entered June 29. Subsequent appellate and collateral decisions are separately dated.
cases.findings: The judgment contains three counts: conspiracy to transport minors for criminal sexual activity, transportation of a minor for that purpose, and sex trafficking of a minor. The court imposed concurrent terms, the longest 240 months.
cases.response: Maxwell challenged the judgment on appeal, including the scope of Epstein's non-prosecution agreement, time limits, jury issues and sentencing. The Second Circuit affirmed on September 17, 2024; the Supreme Court denied her petition on October 6, 2025.
cases.outcome: The reviewed August 25, 2026 district-court order separately denied her post-conviction petition. The conviction and 20-year sentence were not vacated by any of these cited decisions.
cases.limitations: This dossier records the cited decisions and their dates, not a guarantee that no further filings exist. Certiorari denial is not a new merits ruling. Maxwell's conviction does not establish guilt of uncharged associates or every person mentioned in released records.

cases.title: Deutsche Bank: NYDFS findings on compliance failures
cases.summary: A New York banking consent order imposed a $150 million penalty for compliance failures involving Epstein and two separate correspondent-bank relationships.

entityRoles.role: regulated bank subject to consent order
bank customer whose accounts were reviewed

cases.statusDetail: Consent order signed July 6, 2020; publicly announced July 7. Findings and remedies are those of the regulator in this order.
cases.findings: NYDFS found unsafe and unsound business conduct and an ineffective anti-money-laundering program. Its Epstein findings include inadequate account monitoring and failure to implement or communicate conditions imposed on the relationship.
cases.response: The bank agreed to the order and continued cooperation with its monitor. Paragraphs 109–111 credit its cooperation, internal investigations and remediation efforts, which the regulator weighed in resolving the matter.
cases.outcome: The order required a $150 million penalty and directed the existing monitor to address the identified failures.
cases.limitations: The total penalty covers Epstein, Danske Estonia and FBME matters together; it is not an Epstein-only fine. Regulatory findings are distinct from a criminal conviction, the separate $75 million civil settlement, and proof that every questioned payment was unlawful.

cases.title: Deutsche Bank: $75 million survivor class settlement
cases.summary: SDNY approved the settlement resolving the survivor class's civil claims against Deutsche Bank.
cases.statusDetail: Order and final judgment, 1:22-cv-10018 (JSR), docket 122, signed October 20, 2023.
cases.findings: The court found the negotiated settlement fair, reasonable and adequate for the class. It did not decide the bank's liability at trial.
cases.response: Paragraph 11 expressly states that the settlement and judgment cannot be treated as admissions or evidence of liability, fault or wrongdoing.
cases.outcome: The judgment specifies a $75 million payment obligation to the settlement fund and dismisses the released claims with prejudice.
cases.limitations: Settlement approval is not a finding that the bank committed the alleged trafficking offenses. This judgment's wording does not itself verify completed payment or distributions to individual claimants.

cases.title: JPMorgan: $290 million survivor class settlement
cases.summary: Final approval resolved the survivor class's civil claims against JPMorgan in a separate action from the US Virgin Islands government's lawsuit.
cases.statusDetail: Final settlement approval in November 2023 in 1:22-cv-10019 (JSR). Hearing held November 9; available judgment reproduction indexed November 13. Month precision is retained.
cases.findings: The court approved the settlement's fairness and adequacy and found the bank had satisfied its fund-payment obligation. These are settlement findings, not a merits verdict establishing the underlying allegations.
cases.response: Paragraph 12 provides that neither settlement nor judgment is an admission or evidence of liability or wrongdoing.
cases.outcome: Paragraph 13 records $290 million paid to the qualified settlement fund. Released claims were dismissed with prejudice; specified individual assault claims against natural persons were not released.
cases.limitations: Payment into the fund is distinct from completed claimant distributions. The $290 million amount is separate from the $75 million USVI settlement. This record does not imply criminal guilt of bank personnel.

cases.title: JPMorgan and USVI: $75 million civil settlement
cases.summary: JPMorgan and the US Virgin Islands government announced a settlement of the government's civil suit concerning the bank's relationship with Epstein.

entityRoles.role: bank customer underlying the civil claims

cases.statusDetail: Agreement-in-principle announcement on September 26, 2023; this record is tied to that announcement, not an assumed later payment date.
cases.findings: The cited announcements establish the agreement and its terms. They do not establish the government's allegations through a trial verdict.
cases.response: JPMorgan said the agreement involved no admission of liability, expressed regret for its association with Epstein, and said it would not have continued the relationship had it believed he was using the bank for his crimes.
cases.outcome: Announced terms totaled $75 million: $30 million for charitable organizations, $25 million for territorial law-enforcement capacity, and $20 million in attorneys' fees.
cases.limitations: Party statements require attribution. The government's description of anti-trafficking measures does not independently establish subsequent implementation. This is a civil settlement, separate from the survivor class settlement.

cases.title: Bureau of Prisons: Inspector General findings on custody failures
cases.summary: DOJ's Inspector General documented serious staff misconduct and operational failures in Epstein's detention at MCC New York.

entityRoles.role: institution whose custody practices were investigated

cases.statusDetail: OIG investigative report 23-085, published June 27, 2023; administrative findings, with a separately described criminal prosecution.
cases.findings: OIG identified failures involving a required cellmate, inmate checks, supervision, record accuracy and security-camera recording. It found falsified records and lack of candor by staff, but no evidence contradicting the FBI's conclusion that no criminal act caused Epstein's death.
cases.response: BOP agreed with all eight recommendations. In its response concerning staffing, BOP stressed failures to perform duties while acknowledging continued recruitment and retention work. OIG required evidence of implementation before closing recommendations.
cases.outcome: The report recommended corrective measures and review of personnel for possible discipline. Two employees' record-falsification charges had been dismissed after compliance with deferred-prosecution agreements; other referrals did not result in prosecutions.
cases.limitations: The review's focus was BOP custody and personnel. Agreement with recommendations is not proof they were implemented. Administrative misconduct does not establish murder or a cover-up, and criminal dismissal does not negate the report's separate findings.

cases.title: DOJ OPR: poor judgment in Epstein non-prosecution decision
cases.summary: DOJ released findings from its professional-responsibility review of the 2006–2008 federal investigation, non-prosecution agreement and treatment of victims.

entityRoles.role: department conducting an internal professional-responsibility review
former U.S. attorney whose decisions were reviewed
subject of the underlying criminal investigation

cases.statusDetail: OPR findings publicly released November 12, 2020, using OPR's professional-misconduct standard.
cases.findings: OPR did not find professional misconduct by DOJ attorneys. It found that Acosta exercised poor judgment in choosing the non-prosecution agreement and in failing to ensure state authorities would notify federally identified victims about the state plea hearing. It also criticized the treatment of victims.
cases.response: DOJ released the executive summary to affected victims and publicly reported both the absence of a professional-misconduct finding and the findings of poor judgment.
cases.outcome: The report supplies an official assessment of prosecutorial decisions and victim communications. The cited public announcement reports no professional-misconduct sanction.
cases.limitations: A finding of poor judgment is not a criminal conviction; absence of professional misconduct under OPR's standard is not a broad exoneration of every decision or practice. This review did not adjudicate every allegation about Epstein, associates or intelligence agencies.

cases.title: MIT: review of post-conviction gifts and institutional response
cases.summary: MIT released its commissioned Goodwin Procter review of donations, campus visits and approval decisions involving Epstein.

entityRoles.role: former laboratory director whose actions were reviewed
faculty member whose actions were reviewed

cases.statusDetail: Institutionally commissioned fact-finding report released January 10, 2020; not a government criminal investigation or court verdict.
cases.findings: The review traced $850,000 in gifts and found serious errors of judgment in accepting post-conviction donations. It said the absence of a controversial-donor policy prevented treating acceptance itself as a policy violation. It separately attributed nondisclosure of gifts to Lloyd.
cases.response: MIT announced paid administrative leave for Lloyd, committed to changes in donor review and reporting systems, and donated $850,000 to organizations supporting survivors.
cases.outcome: A December 2020 presidential update described reforms completed or underway and additional recommendations still being developed.
cases.limitations: Findings are attributed to MIT's commissioned review and limited to its stated donation, leadership and campus-visit scope. They do not establish that recipients participated in Epstein's sexual crimes or independently prove that later reforms worked.

cases.title: Harvard: institutional review, sanctions and later proceedings
cases.summary: Harvard's review examined Epstein's gifts, visiting-fellow appointment and relationship with the Program for Evolutionary Dynamics, identifying gaps in institutional policy and oversight.

entityRoles.role: program director later subject to university discipline
donor, former visiting fellow and campus visitor examined

cases.statusDetail: University review published May 1, 2020. Later discipline, restoration and renewed review are separately dated events; this label is not a statement that the 2020 inquiry remains open.
cases.findings: The university found no accepted gifts from Epstein after his 2008 conviction, but identified weaknesses in gift communications, visiting-fellow screening and aspects of his program access. Continued association by itself was not a policy violation under the rules then in place.
cases.response: Harvard redirected $200,937 in unspent gifts to survivor-support organizations and ordered policy work. A later faculty review led to program closure and two-year restrictions for Nowak.
cases.outcome: A department chair confirmed restoration of Nowak's privileges in March 2023. In February 2026, the university confirmed a separate paid leave pending review of newly released records.
cases.limitations: The 2020 report was an institutional review, not a criminal judgment. The 2026 leave was pending review rather than a new misconduct finding, and no later outcome was verified. Neither campus contact nor mention in released files establishes criminal complicity.

coverage.title: Epstein: cases, institutions and public records
coverage.summary: Criminal case history; institutional reviews; AI-research donations; a specifically documented campus meeting; banking and civil settlements; public disclosure milestones.
notes: status: Selected, source-checked research; not an exhaustive archive
date Precision: YYYY or YYYY-MM values preserve the source's available precision. For ranges, the date is the beginning unless the text identifies an endpoint.

evidence Meaning: Documented means the cited source directly records the event, relationship or attributed institutional finding. It does not convert an allegation in a document into established fact.
The full multi-million-page corpus, all correspondence, all flight entries and all claimed dinner or lunch attendees were not reviewed.
No complete or authenticated criminal 'client list' is asserted.
No Epstein–CIA, Epstein–Mossad, Epstein–BlackRock, Epstein–Blackwater or state-control edge was established by this selected research.
The dataset does not reproduce disputed sexual allegations against uncharged third parties.
The $75 million Deutsche Bank survivor settlement and additional estate or other-bank settlements require their own source and procedural-status review before addition.

Later challenges to commissioned-review conclusions and congressional inquiries should be added as separately attributed developments, with responses, rather than silently replacing the original findings.
A document mention, flight log, address-book entry, meeting, photograph or donation is not proof of criminal conduct.
Convictions, untried indictments, civil allegations, settlements, regulator findings and commissioned reviews are different evidence categories.
DOJ says the 2026 corpus includes potentially false submissions from members of the public; a DOJ-hosted file is not automatic authentication of its assertions.
No victim names, private contact details, addresses or graphic material are included.
Do not infer connections to intelligence agencies, countries or ethnic or religious communities from the relationships shown here.
Leon Black, Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone and Blackwater are distinct names and organizations; similar wording is not evidence of a connection.

coverage.title: History, AI and public affairs
coverage.summary: Selected, dated public records across historical institutions, asset management, private security, intelligence oversight, AI, conservative organizations, and specific state institutions. Not an exhaustive historical or membership database.
notes: period: from: 1600; to: 2026-10-19
topics: Historical institutions Finance & companies Intelligence & conflict AI & technology Politics & media

included: East India Company charter, parliamentary regulation and transfer of governing powers; Bank of England ownership; Federal Reserve Act; Bretton Woods; UN partition recommendation. CIA creation, documented Iran and Guatemala interventions, Church Committee, MKULTRA hearing and CIA detention-study release. BlackRock founding, Ukraine advisory discussions and AI infrastructure partnership; partial Blackwater/Xe–Academi–Constellis lineage; Nisur Square prosecution and pardons. Dartmouth AI proposal, NVIDIA, In-Q-Tel, Palantir incorporation and founder governance, DeepMind, OpenAI launch supporters, Microsoft, Anthropic, AWS, MGX and GIP partnerships. TPUSA, Charlie Kirk, Candace Owens, BLEXIT, Erika Kirk, Turning Point Action and documented PROCLAIM/BIBLEin365 professional connections. Ukraine ministry procurement, Israeli Finance Ministry Nimbus procurement, Russian GRU indictment, Wagner sanctions, UN Ukraine resolution and ICC warrants.
counts: sources: 46; entities: 76; events: 50; relationships: 63
Historical precedents are context, not proof of an unbroken hidden network linking every institution.
BlackRock is an asset manager, Blackwater a security-business lineage; similar names supply no evidence of affiliation.
Constellis acquired selected predecessor businesses, not all Blackwater assets or intellectual property. Its account says Erik Prince does not own Constellis.
Country labels must not imply collective guilt; the graph uses ministries, agencies, governments and named individuals.
Contracts, funding, attendance, employment and advisory roles are distinct. A connection is not evidence of conspiracy or complicity.
No claim is made that Erika Kirk or TPUSA has an intelligence or criminal affiliation. Unsupported assassination and trafficking rumors were excluded.
No complete roster of covert personnel or “all AI companies” is claimed; public records cannot establish that scope.
Official organizational pages establish announced roles and transactions, not independent verification of self-promotional performance claims.
Arrest warrants, indictments and sanctions are labeled separately from convictions. Records describe historical actions, not necessarily current case status.
The IQT–Palantir investment is widely reported but was not included as a dated edge because this pass did not locate a primary source establishing date and terms.
No claimed Palantir–Israeli Defense Ministry operational edge was added from a company media index; the Nimbus procurement edges use direct government/vendor records.
Events with year or month precision are not assigned invented days; access-date relationships are explicitly marked as observations.

coverage.title: Corporate cases: documented actions and contested claims
coverage.summary: Eleven selected SEC, FTC, DOJ, court and DOL matters involving finance, technology, privacy and employment. Case dates identify specific actions. Company responses and later developments are recorded separately.
notes: This selection is not a comprehensive corporate misconduct database. Absence does not establish a clean record.
Regulatory findings, allegations, consent settlements and trial findings have different meanings. A documented settlement does not make every complaint allegation a proved fact.
No liability is inferred from attendance, investments, employment, corporate-group membership or other relationships.
BlackRock Advisors and BlackRock, Inc. are distinct respondents. Amazon’s existing atlas entity combines the parent and AWS; case roles specify services and defendants.
Google’s judgment is under documented appellate challenge; this edition verifies filings rather than asserting an exhausted appellate outcome.
Cases on AI suppliers can concern securities or employment rather than AI itself. Alexa and Ring have specific algorithm/data-use allegations.
Primary DOL decree indexed text was available, but direct PDF retrieval returned 403; the limitation is recorded in the source entry.
No private complainant identities, contact details, raw customer data or personal victim records are reproduced.

coverage.title: State, intelligence and security accountability records
coverage.summary: Ten bounded case histories based on official investigations, court records, sanctions decisions and negotiated resolutions; reviewed 19 October 2026.
notes: This is a selected case collection, not a complete history of covert operations or all alleged misconduct.
Each status describes the dated record specified in statusDetail. Investigative findings, sanctions and indictments are not interchangeable with convictions.
Officials, investigators, courts, defendants and program operators have explicit case roles. An entity's appearance does not imply culpability.

Most sources are primary government records. The reported September 2015 dismissal of the Academi deferred charges is attributed to a reproduced Intercept report; the final court order was not retrieved.
Redacted or destroyed records limit reconstruction. No inference of undisclosed networks, contemporary mind-control operations, or collective responsibility is drawn.

coverage.title: Epstein: institutional accountability and case outcomes
coverage.summary: Nine dated dossiers distinguishing a criminal conviction, a banking regulatory action, three civil settlements, two DOJ oversight reviews and two university reviews. Ten additional procedural or institutional-response events supplement the existing atlas; existing entities and source IDs are reused.
notes: Case status is attached to the specified action and date. It does not automatically assert the latest legal or employment status.

Institutionally commissioned reviews are explicitly identified. The shared official-investigation status is used for them as well as government reviews, with the distinction preserved in statusDetail.
Settlement amounts, fund payments, claimant distributions and findings of liability are separate concepts. No-admission provisions are retained.
JPMorgan final approval is preserved at November 2023 precision because the hearing date and the available reproduction's indexed date differ and the signed docket date was not independently pinned.

The prison-record case uses January 3, 2022, its dismissal filing date. Its prosecutor's recommendation was dated December 13, 2021. The later OIG narrative uses that December date; the distinction is recorded rather than silently harmonized.
No names or private details of victims, witness contact information, graphic descriptions, or purported comprehensive client list are included.
No inference of criminality follows from a donation, meeting, document mention, institutional affiliation or graph edge. Entity roles distinguish subjects from investigators and civil plaintiffs.
This is selected accountability research, not review of the full Epstein document corpus or every later court filing. The separate 2026 Harvard review has no verified outcome in this extension.
